vignette:
Mai Pham is a 71-year-old divorced financial analyst who lives alone in a quiet suburban apartment. Three years ago, while leaving her office building late one evening, she was abducted from the parking garage by two men who forced her into a van and held her captive in a basement for four days. She had been working late on a quarterly report, a habit she had kept for decades, and no one noticed her missing until the next morning. During the captivity, she was blindfolded, bound, and repeatedly threatened; she was told that if she did not cooperate with a ransom demand, she would never see her family again. She managed to free herself on the fourth day when her captors became careless, fleeing through a back door and running to a gas station to call for help. The police who arrived initially treated her with suspicion, asking pointed questions about whether she knew her captors. No one was ever arrested, and the case was closed within weeks. Mai was left with the conviction that the institutions she had trusted-the police, her employer's security systems-had simply failed her.

In the months that followed, Mai found herself unable to stop thinking about what might have been. She would lie awake at night, replaying the moment she had stayed late at the office, calculating how her life would be different if she had just gone home on time that evening. She began to try very hard not to think about the details of the captivity itself-the smell of the basement, the pressure of the blindfold-but the counterfactuals kept surfacing, unbidden, as if her mind were punishing her. She started to delay sleep deliberately, staying up until two or three in the morning, because the darkness made her feel more vulnerable. She had always been a light sleeper, but now she found it harder to feel safe at night than during the day; she would check the locks on her apartment door three or four times before finally lying down, and even then she kept a small lamp on.

At work, Mai continued to function as a financial analyst, but her environment had become a minefield. The parking garage where she had been taken became impossible to enter. She now parks in a surface lot two blocks away, even in bad weather, and she leaves the office long before dusk, often cutting meetings short. Her cubicle, tucked into a corner on the seventh floor, has become her only real safe zone. She has told her supervisor she prefers to work from that spot and rarely moves around the building. Outside of work, she feels safe only in her own apartment, and even there, the sense of contamination from the captivity clings to her. She showers twice a day, sometimes three times, and still feels dirty, as if the residue of the basement will never wash off. She has stopped going to the grocery store after dark, and she no longer meets friends for dinner because being out in public after sunset triggers an overwhelming wave of fear and anger.

The slightest upset now feels unmanageable. A minor error in a spreadsheet, a raised voice in the hallway, or an unexpected phone call can send Mai into a spiral of anxiety. She has come to believe that she cannot cope with even the most ordinary stress, and this belief has made her withdraw from colleagues and neighbors. She has not told anyone at work about the captivity; she sees their everyday interactions as proof that they cannot understand what she endured, and she is certain that if they knew, they would see her as damaged. Her isolation has grown. She has stopped attending the weekly lunches she once enjoyed with her fellow analysts, and her relationship with her adult daughter, who lives in another state, has become strained because Mai refuses to travel or to have her daughter visit overnight-she cannot bear the thought of anyone else being in her apartment at night, when her vigilance is highest.

Mai finally sought help after a particularly bad week. She had snapped at a junior analyst who touched her shoulder to get her attention, and her supervisor had gently suggested she take some time off. Now, sitting in a therapist's office, Mai is afraid that she is losing her grip on the life she built after the divorce twenty years ago. She hopes that talking about what happened might make the sense of contamination go away, but she is equally terrified that reliving the memory will break her. She wants to feel safe at night again, to stop calculating the life she might have lived, and to believe that she can handle an ordinary upset without falling apart.
